title: 416. Trigonometry & Periodic Models: Pythagorean Trigonometric Identities
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise the basic identity linking sine and cosine.
questions.question: Which equation is true for every angle \(\theta\)?
questions.explanation: A point \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\) on the unit circle satisfies \(x^2+y^2=1\), so \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) for every \(\theta\). The equation without squares fails, for example, at \(\theta=45^\circ\), where \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\sqrt{2}\).
questions.hint: Use the equation of the unit circle, and test the other equation at \(\theta=45^\circ\).

questions.learningObjective: Recognise the Pythagorean identity that involves tangent.
questions.question: Wherever both sides are defined, \(1+\tan^2\theta\) equals which expression?
questions.explanation: Divide \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) by \(\cos^2\theta\): \(\tan^2\theta+1=\frac{1}{\cos^2\theta}=\sec^2\theta\). The expression \(\csc^2\theta\) equals \(1+\cot^2\theta\), which comes from dividing by \(\sin^2\theta\) instead.

questions.concept: Cosine from sine in Quadrant II
questions.learningObjective: Use the Pythagorean identity and the quadrant to find a cosine.
questions.question: An angle \(\theta\) in Quadrant II has \(\sin\theta=\frac{3}{5}\). What is \(\cos\theta\)?
questions.explanation: From \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\): \(\cos^2\theta=1-\frac{9}{25}=\frac{16}{25}\), so \(\cos\theta=\pm\frac{4}{5}\). In Quadrant II cosine is negative, so \(\cos\theta=-\frac{4}{5}\).
questions.hint: The identity gives two possible values; the quadrant decides the sign.

questions.learningObjective: Rewrite an expression using the basic Pythagorean identity.
questions.question: Which expression equals \(1-\cos^2\theta\) for every angle \(\theta\)?
questions.explanation: Rearranging \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) gives \(\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta\). The sign is positive; \(-\sin^2\theta\) equals \(\cos^2\theta-1\), the opposite difference.
questions.hint: Rearrange the basic identity so that the given expression stands alone on one side.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise the Pythagorean identity that involves cotangent.
questions.question: Wherever both sides are defined, \(1+\cot^2\theta\) equals which expression?
questions.explanation: Divide \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\) by \(\sin^2\theta\): \(1+\cot^2\theta=\frac{1}{\sin^2\theta}=\csc^2\theta\). The expression \(\sec^2\theta\) pairs with tangent, not cotangent.

questions.concept: Tangent from secant in Quadrant II
questions.learningObjective: Use the tangent-secant identity together with a quadrant to find a tangent.
questions.question: An angle \(\theta\) in Quadrant II has \(\sec\theta=-\frac{5}{3}\). What is \(\tan\theta\)?
questions.explanation: From \(\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta-1\): \(\tan^2\theta=\frac{25}{9}-1=\frac{16}{9}\), so \(\tan\theta=\pm\frac{4}{3}\). In Quadrant II sine is positive and cosine is negative, so tangent is negative: \(\tan\theta=-\frac{4}{3}\).
questions.hint: Use \(1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta\), then choose the sign of tangent for the quadrant.

questions.learningObjective: Simplify a product of conjugate factors with a Pythagorean identity.
questions.question: Which expression equals \((1-\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)\) for every angle \(\theta\)?
questions.explanation: Multiply as a difference of squares: \((1-\sin\theta)(1+\sin\theta)=1-\sin^2\theta\). By the Pythagorean identity, \(1-\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta\). The expression \(1+\sin^2\theta\) has the wrong sign on the squared term.

questions.concept: Sum of squares at complementary angles
questions.learningObjective: Combine the cofunction relation with the Pythagorean identity.
questions.question: What is the exact value of \(\sin^2 40^\circ+\sin^2 50^\circ\)?
questions.explanation: Since \(50^\circ=90^\circ-40^\circ\), \(\sin 50^\circ=\cos 40^\circ\). The sum becomes \(\sin^2 40^\circ+\cos^2 40^\circ=1\) by the Pythagorean identity.
questions.hint: The two angles are complementary; rewrite one sine as a cosine.

questions.concept: Product from a sum of sine and cosine
questions.learningObjective: Square a sum of sine and cosine and apply the Pythagorean identity.
questions.question: An angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\sin\theta+\cos\theta=1.2\). What is \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\)?
questions.explanation: Square both sides: \(\sin^2\theta+2\sin\theta\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta=1.44\). Since \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1\), this gives \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta=0.44\), so \(\sin\theta\cos\theta=0.22\). The value \(0.44\) is twice the required product.
questions.hint: Square the given equation and replace \(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta\) by \(1\).

questions.learningObjective: Simplify a quotient by applying two Pythagorean identities.
questions.question: Wherever it is defined, \(\frac{\sec^2\theta-1}{\sec^2\theta}\) equals which expression?
questions.hint: Split the fraction into two terms, or replace the numerator using \(1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta\).
